item.title: StackOverflow now gets fewer than 1000 questions a month
item.description:
Source: data.stackexchange.com

Top Comment:

What is this "Stack Overflow" you speak of?

Oh yes. Now I remember. I used to visit the site every day.

I love helping my fellow developers and answering their questions whenever I can.

My reputation there is 29,020, and I've contributed 645 quality answers.

I used to brag about this.

Now I had to think a bit to remember SO still exists.

My last answer was on May 28, 2021, over five years ago.

Obviously it wasn't LLMs that drove me away. And I'm not sure what it was.

Was it the culture, as others here pointed out? Or did I just get busy with other things?

---

Update: Now I think I remember what muted my enthusiasm.

Some of you older programmers may have used jQuery.

There is a common convention to use $ as the first character of a variable name that is a jQuery object:

  var $foo = $('#foo');
One of my few claims to fame is that I invented that convention and promoted it on the early jQuery mailing list.

Someone asked about this:

https://stackoverflow.com/questions/205853/why-would-a-javas...

The top-rated answer, with 1542 votes, is a good summary.

The second answer, with 278 votes, is as irrelevant as an answer can be.

I'm in third place with 71 votes. I gave the story behind the naming convention, because I like people to know the "how and why".

It gets better! This question was marked as a duplicate of another one. That other question has a wild variety of answers, but none that does what I tried to do: explain the reason and background for the convention.

Ah well. It was fun while it lasted.

item.title: H.264 Is Magic (2016)
item.description:
Source: sidbala.com

Top Comment:

Had the pleasure of working with Jason Garrett-Glaser (better known as DarkShikari) circa 2011 on a patch for x264 to better utilize more cores (slice-threaded lookahead). At the time he was working with Sony to optimize their PlayStation game streaming service, and this had the potential to lower encoding latency (critical to game streaming) even on same-core systems by spreading the frame over more cores to do more parallel work, and doing more intelligent scheduling and convergence after that tile-based work was reconverged into a frame. At the time we were using servers with 48 physical cores to do transcoding, a bit of a rarity in a single NUMA space back then and there were no instances to test this on so I flamegraph traced a few encodes at very high thread parallel counts and send back the instrumented profiles (from a custom compiled version) showing the core work being done and he used that to optimize the motion estimation code which worked on the first shot to perfectly level out cpu usage and increase encoding speed across ~24 cores (was previously topping out around 8 and running one core hot iirc). I got a look into how exotic and complex this project was, particularly in terms how low level and advanced things like motion estimation, quantizing and perceptual compression were... it was and still is sort of magic how many smart techniques are baked into something that we barely pay attention to. They were, even at that time, working on x265.

His blog, Diary of an x264 developer, was a great read too for anyone wanting to get a vantage point on how crazy that codebase was.

[1]https://github.com/mstorsjo/x264/blob/master/doc/threads.txt

(edit: was Gaikai that was acquired by Sony in 2012 and is the basis for PlayStation Now)

item.title: If-then-else had to be invented (2020)
item.description:
Source: github.com

Top Comment:

The submitted title

> The 'else' keyword is probably a literal translation from German (2020)

is editorialised, inaccurate, and very misleading.

The actual title: “if … then … else had to be invented!”

And the content doesn’t say anything about it being a literal translation from German; rather:

> What they do say is that this document was originally written in German and hastily translated into English. I think a carefully-chosen German word was probably translated as an archaic English word and then never revisited.

Wild speculation, and definitely nothing about literality of translation.

As for the author’s description of it being archaic, well, I’d call that misleading too. Bare “else”, arguably (definitely not colloquial in most dialects), but as “or else”, perfectly current.

Seems perfectly reasonable to me that someone considered the options, decided “otherwise”, “or else” too wordy and confusing in its own way, and so settled on bare “else” as the best choice (which I think it is), not how people mostly speak, but perfectly legitimate, and concise.

(In other words: I think we’d have settled on “else” even without the possible German step. This too is speculation, of course.)
